payload_fields.productDetailsTitle: Glow: Three Components, No Stated Quantities, and One Unresolved Identity
payload_fields.productDetailsDescription:
Glow is a multi-component product, and the first thing to establish is what can and cannot be said about its contents.

It has no molecular formula, no molecular weight and no CAS registry number, because a mixture of several compounds does not have them. Any document quoting a single formula or molecular weight for this product is describing something other than what is in the vial. Each component has to be considered on its own identifiers, which are set out on the individual component pages in this catalogue.

The composition commonly marketed under this name is GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500. That is stated here as the commonly marketed composition, not as a verified fact about this product — the distinction matters, and no ratios are invented on this page because none are available to state.

Which brings up the most basic specification gap. The product listing gives a variant of "Standard" and **no component quantities whatsoever**. Not a total mass, not individual masses, not a ratio. For a product whose entire proposition is a specific combination of three substances, this means the proposition itself is unstated. No molar calculation of any kind is possible. No concentration can be prepared to a known value. No published protocol concerning any component can be matched. A researcher cannot even determine whether the components are present in roughly equal amounts or whether one predominates. This should be resolved with the supplier before any use, and it is a more fundamental gap than any of the analytical questions that follow from it.

A partial reconstruction is possible from the repository's own catalogue data, and it is worth setting out because it is reproducible rather than assumed. The file "lib/masterCatalogData.ts" lists a corresponding spray presentation under the SKU "SPR-GLOW-70MG", giving a **total fill mass of 70 mg**. The individual components are sold in this same catalogue at fixed strengths: GHK-Cu at 50 mg or 100 mg, BPC-157 at 5 mg or 10 mg, and TB-500 at 5 mg or 10 mg. Enumerating every combination of those offered strengths gives exactly one that sums to 70 mg: **GHK-Cu 50 mg + BPC-157 10 mg + TB-500 10 mg**. The alternatives land on 60, 65 or 110 mg and are excluded.

Two caveats keep this an inference rather than a fact. The 70 mg figure describes the spray line, not this vial, and "masterCatalogData.ts" is demonstrably stale — its prices differ from the current supplied price list, and its images point at inherited assets the application now blocks. So this is the most probable composition on the available evidence, derived by a method the reader can check, and it still requires supplier confirmation.

The second problem is inherited, and it is documented in full on the TB-500 page in this catalogue. "TB-500" is applied in commerce to two chemically different substances: full-length thymosin beta-4, a 43-residue protein with molecular formula C212H350N56O78S and a molecular weight of approximately 4963 g/mol (PubChem CID 45382195), and the short acetylated fragment Ac-LKKTETQ at approximately 889 g/mol. These differ in mass by roughly a factor of 5.6. Both candidates are now fully characterised, though only via CAS number rather than by name: full-length thymosin beta-4 is CAS 77591-33-4 (CID 16132341), and the acetylated fragment is CAS 885340-08-9 (CID 62707662, C38H68N10O14, MW 889.0). Name-based lookups return nothing for either. Which of the two is present in this product is not stated.

The governing principle applies: **a blend cannot be better characterised than its least-characterised component.** Combining two reasonably well-defined peptides with one whose molecular identity is unresolved does not dilute the uncertainty; it imports it into a vial where the components cannot be examined separately without analytical work. Together with the absence of any stated quantities, this is why the page carries a BLOCKED status.

The third issue is specific to this product rather than inherited, and it is the most chemically interesting thing on the page.

A chemical point applies to any vial combining a copper complex with other peptides, and it is the most substantive concern specific to this product rather than inherited from its components. GHK-Cu is a copper(II) complex — the copper is the point of the molecule, not an impurity. Copper(II) is a redox-active transition metal and a well-established catalyst of oxidative reactions in peptides and proteins: it catalyses thiol oxidation to disulfides, and it participates in metal-catalysed oxidation of susceptible residues including methionine and histidine. Placing a redox-active metal complex in the same vial as peptides carrying oxidation-sensitive residues raises a real compatibility question. If the TB-500 component is the full-length protein, its molecular formula contains a sulfur atom, indicating a cysteine and therefore a free thiol or disulfide — precisely the chemistry copper catalyses. No stability or compatibility study for this combination is supplied, and none is claimed here. Components individually stable are not thereby stable together, and a certificate issued at release says nothing about what the vial contains after a period of storage.

A fourth consideration applies to fixed-ratio blends generally and is worth stating because it bears directly on whether this product is suitable for research at all. A pre-mixed three-component vial forecloses the experimental design that would be needed to learn anything from it. Demonstrating that a combination does something its components do not requires component-alone arms alongside the combination and a vehicle control — and for three components, a full factorial design requires eight arms. A pre-mixed vial can supply exactly one of them. It cannot produce a component-alone control, cannot vary one component while holding the others constant, and cannot produce any ratio other than whatever it contains. A laboratory wishing to study these three peptides together would need to source them separately, in which case this product offers nothing experimentally.

A naming note. This product appears as Glow, Glow blend, and occasionally as a "glow stack" or similar cosmetic-oriented designation. Each component carries its own disambiguation requirements, documented on its own page: GHK-Cu is copper tripeptide-1 and is distinct from AHK-Cu, also in this catalogue; BPC-157 is also written as body protection compound 157 and relates to PL-14736; and TB-500 relates to thymosin beta-4, which must not be confused with thymosin alpha-1, an entirely different molecule with its own approvals in some countries. The Klow product in this catalogue is commonly marketed as this same combination with KPV added.

The material is supplied as a lyophilised powder in a sealed glass vial. The stated quantity refers to the mass of material in the vial. Lyophilised peptides are hygroscopic, so the usual laboratory convention is to allow a sealed vial to reach room temperature before opening it, so that atmospheric moisture does not condense onto cold powder. Amino Based publishes no product-specific stability study for this material, so no shelf-life, reconstituted-stability or freeze-thaw tolerance figures are claimed here; where such data are needed for a protocol they should be established in the receiving laboratory or taken from a lot-specific certificate. The product listing states a variant of "Standard" and no component quantities, so no statement about the molar content of this presentation is possible.
payload_fields.researchFocusTitle: No Combination Evidence, and a Design That Cannot Generate Any
payload_fields.researchFocusDescription:
The research position for this product can be stated briefly and honestly: **no evidence for this combination, as distinct from its components, was identified.** No study examining GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 together against each alone, or against pairwise combinations, was found in the indexed literature.

What exists is evidence about each component separately, and that evidence belongs on the component pages rather than being restated here. In summary, with the detail and the caveats on each page: GHK-Cu has a literature concerning skin and wound biology, with the important qualification documented on its page that the most frequently cited review was authored by investigators affiliated with a company selling GHK products, which is directly relevant to its strongest claims. BPC-157 has a genuine if limited clinical record, including the PL-14736 development programme and a phase I trial in 42 healthy volunteers that completed in March 2016 with no results posted. TB-500's applicable evidence depends on the unresolved question of which molecule it is, and the clinically suggestive findings for thymosin beta-4 come from study designs that are not administration studies — an observational cohort of patients' own endogenous levels, and transgenic mice engineered to overexpress the protein from conception.

So the evidence base for this product is three components of varying and individually qualified support, and nothing whatsoever about the three together.

That gap cannot be filled by reasoning from the components, and the reason is worth working through because it applies to every multi-component product. The claim implicit in selling a three-peptide blend is that the combination is better than its parts. Establishing that requires showing an effect the parts do not produce, which requires an experimental structure the blend cannot supply. For two components the minimum is four arms — A alone, B alone, A+B, vehicle. For three components a full factorial is eight arms: vehicle, three singles, three pairs, and the triple. Only that structure distinguishes genuine interaction from the possibilities that one component is doing all the work, that the effects are merely additive, or that one component is interfering with another.

A pre-mixed vial provides one of those eight arms. It therefore cannot, even in principle, be used to demonstrate the proposition it is sold on. And without component-alone comparators, any positive observation with this product is uninterpretable — consistent with synergy, with additivity, with a single active component, and with partial antagonism between components.

There is a further and more specific reason to be cautious about combining these particular components, which goes beyond the general argument. As set out above, GHK-Cu is a copper(II) complex, and copper(II) is a redox-active metal that catalyses thiol oxidation and metal-catalysed oxidation of susceptible residues. Most multi-component criticisms in this catalogue concern experimental design or mechanistic overlap — the Semax + Selank blend, for instance, delivers roughly double the Pro-Gly-Pro moiety because both components share that tail. Here the concern is chemical: one component is a catalyst for reactions that can degrade the others. That is a sharper objection than mechanistic redundancy, because it means the vial's contents may change over time in a way a release certificate would not capture. No stability study for this combination is supplied.

The limitations in summary: the composition itself is unverified; no component quantities are stated at all, making every calculation impossible; the identity of one component is unresolved by a factor of roughly 5.6 in mass; copper content and stoichiometry are unstated for a redox-active metal complex; compatibility of that complex with oxidation-sensitive peptides over time is unaddressed; no evidence exists for the combination; and the fixed-ratio format prevents generating any. Each component's own limitations are inherited in full.

For a laboratory, the constructive position is that the underlying question — whether agents acting on different aspects of tissue repair and skin biology combine usefully — is reasonable, but that this product cannot address it. Resolving the TB-500 identity by mass spectrometry, which a 5.6-fold mass difference makes trivial, and obtaining actual component quantities, are the minimum prerequisites for using this vial for anything quantitative. Beyond that, separately sourced components with verified identities and known masses, assembled into a factorial design, is what would answer the question — and would also permit the copper compatibility issue to be controlled rather than confounded.
payload_fields.qualityPurityTitle: Analytical Verification for a Three-Component Blend With No Stated Quantities
payload_fields.qualityPurityDescription:
Amino Based publishes analytical results on a per-lot basis. Where a lot-specific certificate of analysis has been issued for this product it is available from the Certificates page, and any purity figure displayed on this page is taken directly from that certificate and stated exactly as recorded. Where no certificate has been published for a lot, no analytical result is claimed for it here, and the absence of a figure should be read as the absence of a published measurement rather than as an implied standard.

Verification of a multi-component blend requires everything that verification of each component requires, plus confirmation of how much of each is present. For this product the second of those cannot even begin, because no quantities are stated.

No single molecular formula, molecular weight or CAS registry number exists for this product, and none is stated here. A certificate quoting any of those for the blend as a whole is describing something other than its contents.

The absence of stated quantities is the primary gap and should be addressed first. The listing gives a variant of "Standard" with no component masses and no ratio. A certificate cannot verify a specification that does not exist, so the first requirement is for the supplier to state the intended composition and quantities; only then can a certificate confirm or refute them.

Identity of the TB-500 component is the second requirement, and it is analytically straightforward. The candidates are full-length thymosin beta-4 at approximately 4963 g/mol and the fragment Ac-LKKTETQ at approximately 889 g/mol — a 5.6-fold difference that any mass spectrometric measurement resolves without difficulty. In a blend of this composition, a mass spectrum should show well-separated species for each component, since GHK-Cu is a small copper-complexed tripeptide, BPC-157 a pentadecapeptide, and the TB-500 component either a heptapeptide or a 43-residue protein. Whichever appears settles the question outright. This is the cheapest decisive test available for this product.

Per-component quantitation is the third requirement. Verifying a stated composition requires a method resolving and quantifying each component independently, with each calibrated against its own authentic reference standard. A single total-peptide figure or a single purity percentage does not establish the composition of a blend and is the specification most commonly missing from blend certificates.

Copper content and speciation is a requirement specific to this product and is easy to overlook. GHK-Cu is a copper(II) complex, so copper is a defining constituent rather than a contaminant. Total copper is readily measured by atomic absorption spectroscopy or inductively coupled plasma methods, and the copper-to-peptide stoichiometry is a meaningful specification: a preparation with excess free copper is chemically different from a properly complexed one, and free copper is both more redox-active and more likely to catalyse degradation of the other components. Neither total copper nor stoichiometry is stated for this product.

Oxidation status of the other components follows directly from the copper question, and it is the check most likely to be missing. Where oxidation-sensitive residues are present — a cysteine thiol, a methionine, a histidine — metal-catalysed oxidation produces mass-shifted species that are detectable but only if sought. If the TB-500 component is the full-length protein, its formula contains a sulfur atom indicating a cysteine, so thiol oxidation and intermolecular disulfide formation are specifically plausible in this chemical environment. Dimeric and oxidised species appear at characteristic masses and will not be detected by a purity figure reported without reference to them.

Stability for the combination is therefore a genuine open question rather than a formality. A certificate issued at release describes the vial at release. Where one component catalyses reactions that degrade others, the composition at the point of use may differ, and no stability study for this combination is supplied or claimed.

Salt forms apply to each peptide component, and lyophilised mass is not peptide content: any stated figures would include counter-ions and residual water, and unless content has been determined specifically they are fill masses.

Amino Based has not performed independent laboratory testing, manufacturing validation, or primary research on this compound beyond what is recorded on any published lot certificate, and makes no claim of third-party accreditation, pharmaceutical-grade manufacture, or regulatory approval for this product.
payload_fields.complianceNoticeTitle: Research Use Only: Unverified Composition, Unresolved Identity, Prohibited in Sport
payload_fields.complianceNoticeDescription:
This product is supplied for laboratory research use only (RUO). It is not for human or veterinary use. It is not a drug, a dietary supplement, a cosmetic, a food or a medical device, and it must not be used in the diagnosis, treatment, cure, mitigation or prevention of any disease or condition in humans or animals. Sale is restricted to qualified researchers, laboratories and scientific institutions. Nothing on this page constitutes medical advice, and no administration, dosing or reconstitution guidance for human or veterinary use is provided here or available on request.

No component of this blend is an approved medicine. Neither GHK-Cu, nor BPC-157, nor full-length thymosin beta-4, nor the Ac-LKKTETQ fragment has been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration or by any other regulatory authority, for any indication, in any jurisdiction. There is no regulator-reviewed labelling, no approved indication, no established dosing, and no post-marketing safety surveillance for any component or for the combination.

Three points specific to this product require direct statement, and together they are why this page carries a BLOCKED status.

First, the composition is unverified. The three-component composition described on this page is the one commonly marketed under this name; it is not verified for this product, and no ratios are asserted here.

Second, **no component quantities are stated at all.** The listing gives a variant of "Standard" with no total mass, no individual masses and no ratio. For a product whose proposition is a specific combination, the proposition itself is unstated — and no molar calculation, no concentration preparation to a known value, and no comparison with any published protocol is possible. This should be resolved with the supplier before any use.

Third, the molecular identity of the TB-500 component is **not resolved**. Two chemically different substances differing in mass by roughly 5.6-fold are both sold under that designation. The full account is on the TB-500 page in this catalogue.

The evidence position should be stated plainly. **No evidence for this combination, as distinct from its components, was identified.** No study examining these three peptides together against each alone, or against pairwise combinations, was found. Demonstrating that a three-component combination is worth using would require a factorial design of eight arms; a pre-mixed vial supplies one of them and therefore cannot, even in principle, establish the proposition it is sold on. Claims for this blend rest on claims about its components, each of which carries its own documented limitations — including, for GHK-Cu, that the most frequently cited review was authored by investigators affiliated with a company selling GHK products.

A chemical caution is specific to this combination. GHK-Cu is a copper(II) complex, and copper(II) is a redox-active metal that catalyses thiol oxidation and metal-catalysed oxidation of susceptible residues. Placing it in a shared vial with peptides carrying oxidation-sensitive residues raises a compatibility question that no supplied data addresses. Copper content and copper-to-peptide stoichiometry are unstated, and no stability study for the combination is supplied.

Anti-doping status is relevant to anyone connected with competitive sport. According to a United States Anti-Doping Agency athlete advisory on the WADA Prohibited List, TB-500 is prohibited under section S2 and thymosin beta-4 is separately listed as prohibited under section S2. Athletes and support personnel should consult the current published WADA Prohibited List directly.

Nothing on this page suggests that this material is suitable for addressing skin ageing, wound healing, injury, tissue repair, hair growth or any other condition in any person. It is not for human use.

Researchers remain responsible for compliance with the law in their own jurisdiction, for institutional review and biosafety approvals where their work requires them, for any import and export controls applying to shipments of research chemicals, and for safe handling and disposal of the material. Labelling a substance "research use only" describes the supplier's intended use and the terms of sale; it is not a determination of legal status and does not exempt a purchaser from applicable law.

Standard institutional practice for handling lyophilised peptide powders applies: appropriate personal protective equipment, handling in a suitable containment environment to avoid aerosolising fine powder, and disposal of vials and residual solutions in accordance with institutional chemical and biohazard waste protocols.

faqs.question: What is in Glow?
faqs.answer: It is commonly marketed as GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 in a single vial. That is stated here as the commonly marketed composition, not as a verified fact about this product. Being a mixture it has no single molecular formula, molecular weight or CAS number, and none is stated — any document quoting one for the blend is describing something other than its contents.

faqs.question: How much of each component does it contain?
faqs.answer: Nothing is stated. The listing gives a variant of "Standard" with no total mass, no individual masses and no ratio. For a product whose entire proposition is a specific combination of three substances, the proposition itself is unstated — so no molar calculation is possible, no concentration can be prepared to a known value, and no published protocol concerning any component can be matched.

faqs.question: Why does it carry a BLOCKED status?
faqs.answer: Three reasons together. The composition is the commonly marketed one rather than a verified one. No component quantities are stated at all. And it contains TB-500, whose designation covers two chemically different substances differing in mass by roughly 5.6-fold, with no indication which is present. A blend cannot be better characterised than its least-characterised component.

faqs.question: Can copper peptides be mixed with other peptides?
faqs.answer: It is a legitimate open question and the most substantive concern specific to this product. GHK-Cu is a copper(II) complex — the copper is the point of the molecule. Copper(II) is redox-active and a well-established catalyst of thiol oxidation and metal-catalysed oxidation of residues like methionine and histidine. Putting it in a shared vial with oxidation-sensitive peptides raises a compatibility question no supplied data addresses.

faqs.question: Is there evidence for the combination?
faqs.answer: No evidence for this combination, as distinct from its components, was identified. No study examining GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 together against each alone, or against pairwise combinations, was found in the indexed literature. What exists is evidence about each component separately, set out on their own pages with their own qualifications.

faqs.question: Why can a pre-mixed vial not demonstrate its own premise?
faqs.answer: Because of how many arms the experiment needs. Demonstrating a combination does something its components do not requires component-alone arms alongside the combination and a vehicle control. For three components a full factorial is eight arms: vehicle, three singles, three pairs and the triple. A pre-mixed vial supplies exactly one of them, so it cannot even in principle establish the proposition it is sold on.

faqs.question: What would a positive result with Glow actually mean?
faqs.answer: Very little on its own. Without component-alone comparators, any positive observation is equally consistent with genuine synergy, with simple additivity, with one component doing all the work while the others contribute nothing, and with one component partially antagonising another. That ambiguity is not a technicality — it is the whole reason component-alone controls exist.

faqs.question: How does the copper concern differ from other blend criticisms?
faqs.answer: It is sharper. Most multi-component criticisms in this catalogue concern experimental design or mechanistic overlap — the Semax + Selank blend, for instance, delivers roughly double the Pro-Gly-Pro moiety because both components share that tail. Here one component is a catalyst for reactions that can degrade the others, which means the vial’s contents may change over time in a way a release certificate would not capture.

faqs.question: What should a certificate of analysis show?
faqs.answer: First, a stated intended composition and quantities — a certificate cannot verify a specification that does not exist. Then an observed mass resolving each component, which settles the TB-500 identity outright at a 5.6-fold difference. Then per-component quantitation against authentic reference standards for each. Then total copper by atomic absorption or ICP, with copper-to-peptide stoichiometry, since excess free copper is both chemically different and more degradative.

faqs.question: How does Glow differ from Klow?
faqs.answer: Klow is commonly marketed as this same combination with KPV added, making it a four-component product. Every limitation documented here applies there as well, with an additional component and a correspondingly larger factorial requirement — sixteen arms for four components. Both products are listed with a variant of "Standard" and no component quantities.
